# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for those looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source alternative, with the core use case being team collaboration and communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to own and control their data, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Element can be more scalable than Slack, especially for large teams, since it can be self-hosted on the user's own servers.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption, while Slack only offers encryption in transit.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations available
* Good mobile app support
* Large user community
* Limited control over data
### Element
* Self-hosted and open-source
* End-to-end encryption
* Customizable and extensible
* Free to use
* Steeper learning curve and requires technical expertise

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations. It's also suitable for teams that don't require a high level of control over their data. On the other hand, Element is a good choice for large teams or organizations that require a high level of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted platform.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data in JSON format using the Slack API.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into Element.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and settings in Element.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its complexity and required technical expertise. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element requires a significant amount of server resources to run smoothly, which can be a challenge for small teams or those with limited technical expertise. However, for teams that value control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted platform, Element is a clear choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't require a wide range of integrations and are looking for a free, self-hosted solution.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that require a high level of control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted platform.
* Large teams (more than 50 users) that require a scalable and customizable solution.
* Teams that require end-to-end encryption and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted platform.
* Teams that are already using other open-source tools and are looking for a communication platform that integrates well with their existing stack.

## FAQ
### Is Element free to use?
Yes, Element is free to use, but it requires a self-hosted server to run, which can incur costs.
### Can I use Element with a small team?
Yes, Element can be used with a small team, but it may require more technical expertise to set up and maintain.
### Does Element have end-to-end encryption?
Yes, Element has end-to-end encryption, which ensures that only the sender and recipient can read the messages.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools?
Yes, Element can be integrated with other tools, but it may require more technical expertise to set up and configure.
### Is Element suitable for large teams?
Yes, Element is suitable for large teams, but it requires a significant amount of server resources to run smoothly.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. Both tools offer real-time messaging, file sharing, and integration with third-party apps, making them ideal for remote teams, enterprises, and businesses of all sizes. The key reason someone would switch from Slack to Mattermost is to gain control over their data and reduce costs, as Mattermost offers a self-hosted option and a free, open-source version.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup Complexity: Mattermost requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, especially for self-hosted deployments, while Slack is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Mattermost is designed to scale horizontally, making it a good choice for large enterprises, while Slack also offers scalable plans but at a higher cost.
* Integration: Mattermost has a more limited set of integrations with third-party apps compared to Slack, which has a large marketplace of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to use and set up
* Large marketplace of integrations with third-party apps
* Scalable plans available
* Good mobile app support
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option gives teams full control over their data
* Free, open-source version available
* Designed to scale horizontally
* Customizable and extensible through plugins and APIs
* Limited set of integrations with third-party apps

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use, have limited technical expertise, and require a wide range of integrations with third-party apps. It's also a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that don't mind paying per user. Mattermost, on the other hand, is a good choice for large enterprises, teams that require full control over their data, and organizations with the technical expertise to set up and configure a self-hosted deployment.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool like Slack Exporter.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either self-hosted or using a cloud provider like AWS or Google Cloud.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to import your Slack data, including channels, users, and messages.
4. Configure any necessary plugins or integrations in Mattermost.
5. Test your Mattermost deployment to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack for many users, offering a self-hosted option and a free, open-source version. However, one specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's search functionality can be limited, especially for large datasets. Based on our analysis, we recommend switching to Mattermost if you're a large enterprise or a team that requires full control over your data, but if you're a small team that prioritizes ease of use and a wide range of integrations, Slack may still be the better choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Large enterprises with over 1,000 users that require full control over their data
* Teams with limited budgets that can't afford Slack's per-user pricing
* Organizations with high security requirements that need to host their own servers
* Development teams that require customizable and extensible communication platforms
* Teams with over 500 users that don't need a wide range of integrations with third-party apps

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost offers a self-hosted option that gives teams full control over their data.
### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost offers a free, open-source version, as well as a self-hosted option.
### Can I integrate Mattermost with third-party apps?
Mattermost has a more limited set of integrations with third-party apps compared to Slack, but it does offer some integrations and a customizable API.
### How do I migrate from Slack to Mattermost?
You can export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool, then import it into Mattermost using the Mattermost import tool.

# Discord vs Element

## Overview

Chat platform popular with gaming and developer communities. is a popular proprietary tool in the communication space. Element is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Discord costs Free / $9.99/month; Element is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Discord is Proprietary; Element is Apache 2.0
- **Data ownership**: Element can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Element eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Element has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Discord

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Element

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [element-hq/element-web](https://github.com/element-hq/element-web) * ~11k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Discord if:** Discord is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Element if:** Element is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Discord in its standard export format, review Element import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Element is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Discord tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Element instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Discord, switching to self-hosted Element will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Discord until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Discord paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Element free to use?
Yes. Element is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Discord to Element?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Discord data, follow the Element import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Element get regular updates?
Yes. Element has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Element without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Element development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Discord](https://discord.com) and [Element](https://element.io) before making decisions.*

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control platforms that help developers manage their codebase. This comparison is beneficial for development teams, especially those considering switching from GitHub to GitLab due to concerns about data ownership or cost. The core use case for both tools is collaborative software development, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their code and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers a free plan with limited features, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with more features.
* Data ownership: GitLab allows users to self-host their repositories, giving them full control over their data, while GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: GitHub has a more straightforward setup process, while GitLab requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms are highly scalable, but GitLab's self-hosted option allows for more flexibility in terms of infrastructure.
* Feature difference: GitLab offers a built-in Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) tool, while GitHub relies on third-party integrations for CI/CD.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Large community of developers
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Limited control over data storage and security
**GitLab:**
* Offers a free self-hosted option with more features
* Gives users full control over their data
* Includes built-in CI/CD tools
* Can be more complex to set up, especially for self-hosting
* Limited support for some third-party integrations

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require a high level of control over their data. It's also a good option for teams that are already invested in the GitHub ecosystem and don't want to switch to a new platform. On the other hand, GitLab is a good choice for larger teams or organizations that require a high level of control over their data and want to self-host their repositories. It's also a good option for teams that want to take advantage of built-in CI/CD tools and don't mind a more complex setup process.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub API or the git clone command.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab and use the GitLab import tool to import your exported repository.
3. Update your local repository to point to the new GitLab repository using the git remote command.
4. Verify that all your repository data, including issues and pull requests, has been successfully imported.
5. Update your team's workflow to use the new GitLab repository.

## Our Take
GitLab is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a robust set of features and a high level of control over data storage and security. However, one technical limitation worth knowing is that GitLab's self-hosted option requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and maintain. For teams that don't require a high level of control over their data, GitHub may still be a better option due to its ease of use and large community of developers.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams that want to self-host their repositories and have full control over their data
* Medium-sized teams that are currently using GitHub's free plan and want to take advantage of more features
* Large teams that require a high level of control over their data and want to use built-in CI/CD tools
* Teams that are currently using GitHub and want to reduce their costs
* Teams that want to use a platform with a more open-source friendly license

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
Yes, GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with more features than GitHub's free plan. However, self-hosting requires a significant amount of technical expertise and infrastructure costs.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to GitLab?
Yes, you can migrate your GitHub repository to GitLab using the GitLab import tool or by exporting your repository using the GitHub API.
### Does GitLab offer CI/CD tools?
Yes, GitLab offers built-in CI/CD tools that can be used to automate testing and deployment of your code.
### Is GitLab suitable for small teams?
Yes, GitLab is suitable for small teams, especially those that want to self-host their repositories and have full control over their data.
### Does GitLab support third-party integrations?
Yes, GitLab supports many third-party integrations, but the selection is not as large as GitHub's.

title: GitHub vs Gitea
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs Gitea

## Overview

The world largest code hosting and collaboration platform. Owned by Microsoft since 2018. is a popular proprietary tool in the developer-tools space. Gitea is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub costs Free / $7-$21/user; Gitea is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: GitHub is Proprietary; Gitea is MIT
- **Data ownership**: Gitea can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Gitea eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Gitea has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Gitea

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [go-gitea/gitea](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea) * ~44k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Gitea if:** Gitea is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from GitHub in its standard export format, review Gitea import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Gitea is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Gitea instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted Gitea will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Gitea free to use?
Yes. Gitea is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to Gitea?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the Gitea import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Gitea get regular updates?
Yes. Gitea has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Gitea without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Gitea development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [Gitea](https://gitea.io) before making decisions.*

* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.

## Our Take
Penpot is still a relatively new and developing tool, and while it shows promise, it may not be production-ready for most users right now. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's scalability features are still in development, and it may not be able to handle very large teams or complex projects. However, for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who value data ownership and control, Penpot is a viable alternative to Figma, and we recommend considering it as an option.

## Who Should Switch

* Startups or individuals who value data ownership and control
* Teams who are already using open-source tools and workflows
* Designers who are looking for a free and customizable design tool
